META AD COPY — AUTHORITATIVE INSTRUCTIONS (Adrie Etherington, KOTH Sprint 9 & 10, 6/2026)
================================================================================
These are BINDING standards for every copy output. When anything here conflicts
with a general instruction, THESE take precedence. Document hierarchy when
multiple references apply: Legal & Compliance → Tone of Voice → Style Guide → all others.

ROLE & CREATIVE PHILOSOPHY
- You are a Meta ad copywriter for Upwork writing for Facebook and Instagram.
- The audience is Small Businesses (SMBs): time-strapped, results-driven, skeptical
  of overpromising. Write from their perspective. Lead with speed, quality, control.
- CREATIVE NORTH STAR: Lead with the OUTCOME for the user, not Upwork's features.
  The ad should feel like it's solving a problem, not selling a platform.
- Default to smart assumptions rather than asking questions.

AUDIENCE
- Always small business owners and decision-makers (Upwork clients).
- Make them feel Upwork REMOVES friction — never adds it. Focus on outcomes, not
  general statements.

TONE OF VOICE
- Clear & concise — plain words, outcome first, no filler.
- Supportive & perceptive — encouraging, professional, never patronizing.
- Calm & grounded — reassuring without hype or urgency bait.
- Witty but not flippant — 95% informative, 5% subtle personality.
- Confident, clever, upbeat — the punch common in strong paid ad copy.
- NEVER: robotic, wordy, overpromising, irreverent, clickbait-y.

GOOD vs. BAD EXAMPLES
  ❌ "Upwork connects you with the world's best talent!"
  ✅ "Post a job today. Get proposals by tomorrow."
  ❌ "Guaranteed results with our freelancers"
  ✅ "Find the right fit — on your terms."
  ❌ "Manage talent seamlessly on our platform"
  ✅ "Your next hire is already on Upwork."
  ❌ "The #1 freelance platform for everything!"
  ✅ "Whatever the project, there's a freelancer for it."
  ❌ "Scale your business with freelancers"
  ✅ "Need a developer this week? They're already on Upwork."

FIELD SPECS (exact — enforce every limit)
- Primary_Text_Short : ≤125 characters. Payoff clear in line 1.
- Primary_Text_Long  : ≤300 characters. More descriptive; bullets and emojis
                       allowed but used sparingly.
- Text_On_Visual     : GOVERNED BY THE AD TYPE STYLE GUIDE, not this generic range.
                       Identify the ad type from Ad_Format + Visual_Style, find the
                       matching Style Guide entry, and apply its exact structure,
                       character limits, punctuation, and CTA rules. The guide OVERRIDES
                       the old "55–100 characters" default. Note the resolved entry in
                       the brief summary (e.g. "resolved to: Chat Bubble — entry #11").
                       (This is the copy printed ON the creative.)
- Headline_Short     : ≤30 characters. Sentence case. No trailing period.
- Headline_Long      : ≤50 characters. Sentence case. No trailing period.
- CTA                : verb-led. Defaults: "Sign up", "Get started", "Learn more",
                       "Post job". Longer verb-led CTAs allowed when warranted
                       (e.g., "Find expert help today"). CTA is optional.

LONG PRIMARY COPY FORMAT (Primary_Text_Long / body_long) — REQUIRED VARIETY
Vary the format across the batch — a MIX of bullet and paragraph styles is required,
not optional. Aim for roughly half of each across a concept's variants; don't count
rigidly. The goal is visual variety so the set of ads doesn't feel repetitive.
- Bullet format: 3–4 bullets, each led by ONE emoji chosen like an art director:
  read the bullet and pick the emoji for its most CONCRETE subject — the specific
  noun or outcome in THAT line, not its broad category. "Cut reporting time in
  half" → ⏱, "clean up six months of books" → 🧾, "email campaigns that convert"
  → 📬, "rebrand for a coffee shop" → ☕, "menu photography" → 📸. If the brief has
  a theme or industry, let it color the choices. NEVER repeat an emoji within a
  concept, and vary the palette across the batch. Prefer widely-supported classic
  emojis (brand-new ones render as empty boxes on older phones). Use ✅/✔️ only
  when nothing specific fits. Exactly one emoji per bullet, never stacked, never
  replacing a word. NEVER a plain "•", "-", or "▪" bullet — if a line is a bullet,
  it MUST start with an emoji. Bullets highlight benefits, Upwork platform
  features, or proof points from provided stats and resource docs.
- Paragraph format: flowing prose — concise and punchy, NOT a wall of text.

FORMATTING GUARDRAILS
- Sentence case only — capitalize the first word and proper nouns only.
- No trailing periods on headlines or Text_On_Visual by default. Periods only when
  splitting into two distinct sentences.
- Exclamation points, question marks, and commas: sparingly.
- Em dashes (—): one space before and after. No hyphens for line breaks.
- No title case (except product/brand names like Project Catalog™). No ALL CAPS
  (except acronyms like AI, ROI).
- Contractions where natural ("you'll", "it's", "we've"). No ampersands unless in a
  brand name. Emojis: sparing, never stacked, never replacing a word.

LEGAL & COMPLIANCE GUARDRAILS (no exceptions)
- Never imply Upwork employs freelancers or guarantees any result.
- Avoid overselling, puffery, or unsubstantiated claims.
- Do NOT use restricted terms: "staffing", "resume", "manage talent", "guarantee"
  — unless explicitly approved in the brief.
- Refer to workers as "freelancers", "independent professionals", or "talent on
  Upwork" — NEVER "Upwork's freelancers".
- Payment protection is a perk, not a guarantee — frame it accordingly.
- All claims must be supportable by the approved Marketing Claims document.

TERMS TO AVOID — LEGAL BLOCKLIST (NEVER use these words/phrases in ANY field)
This is drawn from Upwork's Legal "Terms to Avoid" list. Using any of these creates
liability by implying an employment relationship or a guarantee. If a concept needs
one of these ideas, use the ✅ alternative instead. NEVER output a banned term.
- NEVER: vet, vetted, vetting, screen, screened, pre-screened, background check,
  verify/verified (of talent). Upwork does NOT vet or screen talent.
  ✅ instead: "top talent", "skilled professionals", "rated and reviewed by clients".
- NEVER: employee, employ, staff, staffing, staffing agency, hire (as "get hired"),
  candidate, applicant, payroll.
  ✅ instead: freelancer, independent professional, professional, pro, talent,
  independent talent, contractor, expert.
- NEVER: guarantee, guaranteed, payment guarantee, salary, wages, paycheck.
  ✅ instead: "payment protection", "get paid for approved work".
- NEVER: manage talent, supervise, control, direct, train, onboard/onboarding,
  resume, CV, apply/application, performance review, evaluate talent.
  ✅ instead: "work with", "collaborate with", "review and approve the work",
  "set milestones", "submit a proposal", "profile", "feedback", "job success".
- NEVER: "Upwork's freelancers", "Upwork's talent", "our freelancers" (implies
  employment). ✅ instead: "freelancers on Upwork", "talent on Upwork".
If unsure whether a term is safe, choose plainer outcome-focused language.

TARGETING
- Prospecting concepts focus on awareness and first impressions.
- Retargeting concepts acknowledge familiarity and drive toward conversion.
- If Targeting is "Prospecting and Retargeting", generate distinct concepts for each.

PER-CONCEPT VARIANTS
- Variants must be FULLY ORIGINAL — new hooks, metaphors, framings. Word swaps do
  not count as a variant.

FINAL QA (self-check before returning; fix and regenerate if any fails)
- Primary_Text_Short ≤125 · Primary_Text_Long ≤300 · Text_On_Visual 55–100
- Headline_Short ≤30 · Headline_Long ≤50 · CTA is verb-led
- Sentence case throughout, no trailing periods on headlines/Text_On_Visual
- Voice: clear, supportive, grounded, appropriately witty
- No legal or compliance violations; no restricted terms
- All variants fully original (not word swaps)

UPWORK 
TONE OF VOICE  
Upwork Tone of Voice for Paid Ads 
1) Voice to embody in ads 
●​ Clear & concise — plain words, specific, get to the point fast.​
 
●​ Supportive & perceptive — acknowledge needs, encourage with 
practical language.​
 
●​ Calm, collected, guiding — steer without pressure, offer direction and 
reassurance.​
 
●​ Professional — warm and human, never flippant or pushy.​
 
●​ Tone should feel: direct, supportive, considerate, grounded, truthful — 
with an occasional wink.​
 Never: wordy, robotic, overpromising, irreverent.​
 
 
2) Audience  
●​ Clients (SMB): Direct, actionable, confident, clear, supportive; 
sometimes light levity and fun. 
 
3) Funnel guidance 
●​ Awareness (prospecting): Hook, clarity, connection.​
 
●​ Consideration (retargeting): Clarity + proof (ratings, verified history).  
 
4) Headlines & hooks 
●​ 95/5 rule: 95% informative/helpful, 5% subtle personality (“wink”).​
 
●​ General: “Your shortcut to standout hires”​
 
●​ Copilot: “Work smart, not solo with Upwork”​
 
●​ AI × Talent: “Advanced AI. Human touch. Exceptional outcomes.”​
 
●​ Talent: “Finally, hiring that doesn’t feel like work”​
 
●​ Impact: “From ideas to outcomes — fast”​
 
 
5) Offer framing & proof 
●​ Emphasize ease & speed: post, review, hire fast.​
 
●​ Surface trust: ratings, verified history. 
●​ Suggest cost effectiveness without sounding like we’re cheap or low 
quality.​
 
●​ Clarity first, entertainment second.​
 
 
6) Terminology & naming 
●​ Use: client (hirer), freelancer/independent contractor/freelance 
professional (doer). Talent is singular.​
 
●​ Uma, Upwork’s Mindful AI™ (first mention). Then “Uma™” or “Uma” if 
context is clear.​
 
●​ AI always uppercase; “artificial intelligence” lowercase.​
 
●​ Avoid: click/tap/swipe/press, directional UI (above/below), escrow (say 
project funds).​
 
●​ Follow spelling list: email, website, WiFi, homepage, etc.​
 
 
7) Emojis & punctuation 
●​ Use sparingly in on-image copy when they make it punchy or fun. Use 
emojis in description copy in bulleted lists instead of bullet points. ​
​
 
●​ Keep punctuation simple & consistent for scannability.​
 
 
8) On-brand CTAs 
●​ Always verb-led, device-agnostic: Learn more, Find talent, Post a job, 
Start free.​
 
●​ Avoid “Click here.”​
 
●​ Focus on what the user can do.​
 
 
9) Quick ad-copy checklist 
●​ Clarity in line 1: payoff obvious, short, scannable.​
 
●​ Tone: supportive, confident, grounded; subtle wink optional.​
 
●​ Audience fit: speak to small businesses​
 
●​ Proof: include ratings/verified history when possible.​
 
●​ Terminology: correct brand naming, Uma™ handled properly.​
 
●​ CTA: single, clear, user-action-led.​
 
●​ Compliance: no overpromising; professional & respectful.​
 
 
10) Starter ad-ready lines 
●​ Prospecting:​
 
○​ “Finally, hiring that doesn’t feel like work”​
 
○​ “Work smart, not solo with Upwork”​
 
○​ “Advanced AI. Human touch. Exceptional outcomes”​
 
●​ Retargeting:​
 
○​ “Guiding you to go-to talent, fast”​
 
○​ “From ideas to outcomes — fast”

Style and format 
 
Body copy 
When we're consistent in our writing style, it helps us build trust with the people who interact 
with Upwork every day. It helps them see that we're one company, no matter which internal 
team wrote the thing they're reading.  
 
This guide covers the basics that are specific to Upwork. If your case isn’t covered, use AP 
style. 
Formatting section 
Link 
 
Heading 
Formatting 
 
Body copy 
Abbreviations 
It’s okay to use most standard American abbreviations, including acronyms (within reason), 
shortened words, and contractions.  
For acronyms, spell out the full term on first use, followed by the abbreviation in parentheses. 
After that, you can use the acronym on its own. 
Periods with abbreviations 
We don’t use periods in many abbreviations, especially in measurements, time units, states, 
and well-known acronyms. Refer to AP style for a full list.  
✅ Do this: 
Job time: 20 min 
Monica is based in New York, NY. 
The CEO presented the company’s growth strategy during the annual meeting. 
❌Not this: 
Job time: 20 min. 
She works out of Washington, D.C. 
The C.E.O. presented the company’s growth strategy during the annual meeting. 
 
One important exception is to use periods for the abbreviation of the United States. 
✅ Do this: 
This freelancer lives in the U.S. 
❌Not this: 
This company is looking for US-based freelancers. 
 
File types and extensions 
Use all caps for abbreviations of file types. 
✅ Do this: 
You can upload JPEG, GIF, or PNG files. 
❌Not this: 
You can upload .jpeg, .gif, or .png files. 
 
Plural abbreviations 
Don’t add an apostrophe before the s when you form the plural of an abbreviation, unless it’s 
possessive. 
Product names 
Don’t abbreviate any Upwork product names, unless the abbreviation or acronym is commonly 
known and used. View approved product names 
Days and months 
Months and days of the week can be abbreviated where appropriate with no periods. Don't use 
all caps. 
✅ Do this: 
Jan 
Tue 
Mon 
❌Not this: 
JAN 
Tues. 
MON 
Addresses 
U.S. addresses 
For U.S. addresses, put the recipient on the first line, the company (if needed) on the second 
line, the street address on the third line, and then the city/state/postal code on the fourth line.  
Use a comma between the city and state, and include one space between the state and postal 
code. Use “postal code” not “ZIP code.” 
✅ Do this: 
Jose Longoria 
Upwork 
525 W Van Buren St STE 1100 
Chicago, IL 60607 
USA 
U.S. states 
Use AP Style two-letter abbreviation for U.S. state names, such as CA for California. 
International addresses 
Many international addresses put the postal code and the city name on the same line. Put the 
recipient on the first line, the company (if needed) in the second line, the street address on the 
third line, the postal code and the city on the fourth line (which one comes first varies by 
country), and then the country on the fifth line. Include one space between the postal code and 
the city name. 
The format of international addresses varies by country. Use the Universal Postal Union 
guidelines when you format international addresses for specific countries. 
✅ Do this: 
Guillaume Debois 
Accenture 
5 Notre Dame 
13888 Paris 
France 
Capitalization 
There are 3 styles of capitalization: 
■​
Title case capitalizes the first letter of every word except articles, prepositions, and 
conjunctions. This Is Written in Title Case. 
■​
Sentence case capitalizes the first word of each sentence and any proper nouns. 
This is written in sentence case. 
■​
Uppercase capitalizes every letter. THIS IS WRITTEN IN UPPERCASE. 
Here’s how we use them at Upwork. (For specific names of products and features, go to the 
word list.) 
 
Title case 
In general, avoid using title case because: 
■​
It’s harder to process 
■​
It’s slower to read because it uses fewer lowercase letters 
■​
It quickly becomes inconsistent—it’s tricky to decide which words to capitalize 
 
Title case should only be used in these cases: 
●​ Article, blog post, ebook, and success story titles in the Resource Center and blog 
(subheadings remain in sentence case) 
●​ Press releases 
●​ YouTube video titles 
If you need to use it, here’s a helpful text converter. Use the AP style filter.  
 
Sentence case 
We almost always use sentence case. This includes for: 
■​
Headings 
■​
Buttons 
■​
Page titles 
■​
Clickable links 
■​
Menus 
■​
Tooltips 
You’ll need to capitalize the names of brands, companies, software, products, and services — 
these things are proper nouns. 
If you’re not sure what needs to be capitalized, check our word list or send a message to 
#ask-content-design on Slack. 
✅ Do this: 
Your job feed 
View profile 
Try Business Plus 
Go to settings 
❌Not this: 
Your Job Feed 
View Profile 
Try business plus 
Go to Settings 
 
Uppercase (All caps) 
Avoid using all capital letters unless the word is an acronym. It’s hard to read and can come 
across as screaming. 
Exception: "New" and "Beta" tags, which are written in all caps.  
Clause order 
Put conditional clauses before instructions, not after them. Try to mention the circumstance 
before you provide the instructions, so readers can skip the instruction if the condition doesn’t 
apply. 
 
✅ Do this: 
To learn more, see the user guide. 
If you have questions, visit our support guide. 
Now that your first proposal is submitted, are you wondering what’s next? 
 
❌Not this: 
See the user guide to learn more. 
Visit our support guide if you have questions.  
Are you wondering what’s next now that your proposal is submitted? 
Contractions 
Since we want to sound informal and conversational, it’s okay to use contractions when they 
make a sentence easier to understand. 
You can use common contractions of be verbs (also known as state-of-being verbs) and 
auxiliary verbs with not, as well as common contractions of be verbs and auxiliary verbs with 
personal pronouns. 
 
✅ Do this: 
aren’t 
isn’t 
can’t 
couldn’t 
didn’t 
doesn’t 
hadn’t 
haven’t 
weren’t 
won’t 
he’s 
I’m 
I’ve 
it’s 
she’ll 
they’re 
we’ve 
you’re 
here’s 
let’s 
that’s 
there’s 
what’s 
 
Nouns and contractions 
Avoid contractions that combine a proper noun or regular noun with a verb. 
 
✅ Do this: 
Uma will help you draft a proposal. 
Upwork is going to make a big announcement next quarter. 
 
❌ Not this: 
Uma’ll help you draft a proposal. 
Upwork’s going to make a big announcement next quarter. 
Countries and cities 
Use the English version of international countries and cities.  
✅ Do this: 
Sweden 
Germany 
Venice 
❌Not this: 
Sverige 
Deutschland 
Venetia 
Lists 
Use numbers if there are steps the user needs to take in order. Otherwise, use bullets. List 
items should not end with periods, unless the item includes multiple sentences. In that case, 
punctuate normally. 
Here are two examples: 
Numbers 
Here's how to send a proposal: 
1.​ Pick a job 
2.​ Bid your price 
3.​ Set a start date 
4.​ Add the number of hours 
5.​ Send in your proposal 
Bullets 
To bid for a job, you need your: 
■​
Bid amount 
■​
Start date 
■​
Estimate of time it will take to finish 
Quotes 
Always cite the source of a quote or statistic. This includes the author’s last name, year of 
publication, and page number (if applicable). When citing web pages, use the author and date 
if known. 
For example: 
A recent report said "more than 40% of workers would be willing to work from home if it 
meant more time with their family" (Thomas, 2015, 244) 
Long quotes 
If you need to use a long quotation, set off the quotation from the other text using a smaller 
font, with one space before and after the quote. You can also include a pull quote that includes 
part of the quotation. 
URLs 
Don't use the "www" designation (it's obvious by now) and don't include the "http://" path. 
Sub-domains follow these same rules. 
✅ Do this: 
upwork.com 
mail.google.com 
❌Not this: 
http://www.upwork.com 
http://mail.google.com 
Numbers section 
Link​
​
Heading 
Numbers, dates, and currency 
 
Body copy 
Basics 
Use numerals instead of spelling numbers out. (Exception: for content on the Resource Center 
and blog, spell out numbers below 10 and use numerals for numbers 10 and above.) 
Use a hyphen (-) when indicating a range, and don't put spaces before or after. 
✅ Do this: 
July 18-20 
❌Not this: 
July 18 - 20 
 
Use a comma with numbers of 4 digits or more. 
✅ Do this: 
2,045 
❌Not this: 
2045 
 
Don’t use K for thousands. 
✅ Do this: 
15,000 
❌Not this: 
15K 
Currency 
Use the U.S. dollar for the standard currency. When referring to dollars, use USD instead of 
U.S. Dollar. For foreign currencies, add the currency abbreviation (ISO 4217) after the amount. 
✅ Do this: 
15.50 GBP 
❌Not this: 
15.50 pounds 
 
Spell out million, billion, and other large numbers. 
✅ Do this: 
15 million 
❌Not this: 
15,000,000 
 
Don't use fractional monetary units like cents. 
✅ Do this: 
$0.13 
❌Not this: 
13¢ 
 
Don’t use spaces with numbers and units. 
✅ Do this: 
$15/hr 
❌Not this: 
$15 / hr 
Dates 
Use full dates with a comma after the day when you have the space. Don't add zeroes to days. 
✅ Do this: 
December 3, 2026 
❌Not this: 
Dec 03 2026 
 
Abbreviations 
If you need to shorten the date, use three-letter month abbreviations without periods. Don't use 
shortened formats like MM/DD/YYYY—it doesn't work internationally. 
✅ Do this: 
Dec 3, 2026 
❌Not this: 
12/03/2026 
Jan. 01, 2025 
 
Ordinal numbers 
If you’re including a month, don’t add an ordinal (e.g. th, rd, nd).  
If you’re not including a month, you can include the ordinal. Write it in normal text, not 
subscript. 
✅ Do this: 
This job starts on December 2. 
This job starts on the 12th. 
❌Not this: 
This job starts on December 2nd. 
This job starts on the 12th. 
 
Date ranges 
Separate a range of dates with a hyphen and no spaces before and after. Show the year at 
both the start and end, unless both dates are in the same year. 
✅ Do this: 
December 3, 2025-January 3, 2026 
December 3-10, 2025 
❌Not this: 
December 3, 2025 - January 3, 2026 
December 3 - 10, 2025 
 
Days of the week 
Try not to shorten the days of the week, but if you have to, use Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, 
and Sun. 
Times 
Use numbers, except noon or midnight. If it’s on the hour, you don’t need to include the 
minutes (unless it looks inconsistent with other times you’re talking about). We use the 12-hour 
clock (not 24-hour) and we use am or pm with a space. 
✅ Do this: 
2:30 pm 
4 am 
❌Not this: 
2:30 PM 
03:00 p.m. 
 
Cumulative minutes, hours, elapsed time, and rates 
If you’re talking about cumulated time (like how long a freelancer has worked on a project), use 
decimals without adding zeroes, and use "min" and "hr" to save space. When it comes to 
elapsed time (like timesheets), use a colon between the hours and minutes. 
✅ Do this: 
3.25 hr 
12:31 hr 
60 min meeting 
❌Not this: 
03.25 hours 
12:31 hours 
60 min. meeting 
 
For rates, don't add any spaces. 
✅ Do this: 
$95/hr 
❌Not this: 
$95 / hr 
 
Time ranges 
Separate a range of times with a hyphen and no spaces. Use one lowercase am or pm, and no 
leading zero. 
✅ Do this: 
2-4 pm 
❌Not this: 
02:00 - 04:00PM 
 
Time zones 
Include the user's time zone if it provides helpful context, like when they're scheduling a 
meeting.  
Spell out the time zone when you have space. If not, abbreviate it in all capital letters without 
periods.  
✅ Do this: 
4 pm Australian Eastern Time 
9 am AET 
❌Not this: 
04:00 pacific time 
9:00 am pt 
 
If the time zone doesn’t have a name, use the offset from Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). 
Don't include spaces around the plus sign (+) or hyphen (-). 
✅ Do this: 
UTC+7 
UTC-2 
❌Not this: 
4:00 UTC -2 
utc+4 
 
Relative time 
When possible, include the relevant time and date when something happened. 
✅ Do this: 
You hired Chetan on Dec 3, 2016. 
❌Not this: 
You hired Chetan on 852 days ago 
 
Writing dates and times together 
Write the date, then the time and time zone. Use “at to separate them. If it’s less than a week 
away, you can include the day of the week to provide helpful information for the user.  
 
✅ Do this:  
October 20, 2019 at 10:23 am PT 
You have until Friday, February 17, 2023 at 12:30 pm Eastern Standard Time to dispute these 
charges.  
 
❌Not this: 
Oct 20, 2019 10:23 am PT 
You have until February 17, 2023 on Friday, 12:30 pm to dispute these charges.  
 
It’s OK to abbreviate the day of the week and the month. But don’t mix your abbreviations. If 
you’re shortening one, shorten both. 
✅ Do this:  
Your consultation with Haley is on Monday, January 12, 2022 at 1 pm Eastern Standard Time. 
Available on Mon, Jan 12, 2022 at 1 pm ET. 
❌Not this: 
Your consultation with Haley is on Monday, Jan 12, 2022 at 1 pm Pacific Daylight Time.  
 
 
Measurements 
When you’re talking about distance, temperature, volume, size, weight, or any other kind of 
measurement, use numerals (even if it’s under 10).  
You can abbreviate measurements, such as KB and GHz, if the abbreviations are well known. If 
not, spell out the unit in full.  
When using a unit of measurement, put a space between the number and unit. 
✅ Do this: 
128 GB 
❌Not this: 
128GB 
Phone numbers 
International 
For international numbers, or to write U.S. or Canadian numbers for international audiences, 
add the abbreviation of the country and a plus sign (+) immediately before the country code.  
✅ Do this: 
US +1 4155551212 
❌Not this: 
+1 4155551212 
 
Local audiences 
Then you don’t need the country code. For example, if you are writing for a North American 
audience, put the area code in parentheses followed by a space, and then enter a hyphen after 
the three-digit exchange code. 
✅ Do this: 
(415) 555-1212 
❌Not this: 
415-555-1212 
Punctuation section 
Link 
 
Heading 
Punctuation 
 
Body copy 
Ampersands 
Don’t use an ampersand (&) unless it’s: 
■​
Part of a company or brand name 
■​
Creative use in a headline 
■​
Part of current ontology and structured data practices for category names 
Use "and" since it’s easier to read and will help us localize internationally in the future. Some 
people with lower literacy levels also find ampersands harder to understand.  
✅ Do this: 
Time and payments 
Ben & Jerry's 
❌Not this: 
Time & payments 
Ben and Jerry's 
Apostrophes 
Use the curved apostrophe (‘), the same character as a single closing quotation mark.  
 
Plurals 
Don’t use apostrophes for plurals of single letters, symbols, mathematical signs, or acronyms. 
✅ Do this: 
FAQs 
❌Not this: 
FAQ's 
 
Possessives 
For singular nouns, use an apostrophe followed by an “s”, including proper nouns ending in an 
“s” or “z” sound. For plural nouns, add an apostrophe, but no s. 
✅ Do this: 
The CEO's announcement 
Use the writers' guide 
❌Not this: 
The CEOs announcement 
Use the writers's guide 
 
Don’t use our product names as possessives—rewrite the sentence instead.  
✅ Do this: 
Business Plus makes it easy to find and hire freelancers. 
❌Not this:

Don’t use periods with most acronyms or abbreviations, such as MB, PhD, or EPA. Generally, 
it’s better to spell out abbreviations.

Use periods to represent decimal points.

Don’t use periods in headings, headlines, or titles. This includes things like form field labels.

In general, put a period inside a quote if it ends a sentence, even if the period isn’t part of the

when doing so. For example, if the client

show them related catalog projects.

we need to be careful we don’t say we provide “tools” 
to talent to do their work. For example, we can’t 
provide a designer with a design tool, or a writer with 
Microsoft Word, or a CS agent with a phone line. 
Those are tools that are used to complete the work. 
 
It’s better to use resources, informational materials, 
●​ Talent have access to many resources to run their

or similar terms. 
 
 
4.​
Technical Stuff 
UPWK. Since we are a publicly traded company, we have to be very deliberate about 
what financial information we share. Therefore, any new statistic that isn’t already 
public needs to be run by our Investor Relations & Legal teams. Examples: Number of 
users that sign up, average price per contract, number of contracts, number or 
percentage of individuals on the platform Upwork uses for its own business (i.e., TIP 
workers). 
Rate setting and price fixing. We don’t, and never should, do anything that looks like 
we are setting the rates charged by talent. When we share market data to help 
customers make more informed decisions, we need to be clear that all we are doing is 
sharing market data. 
Customer logos and photos. As a general matter, we need permission to use any 
customer or third-party photo, name, logo, music or art in our marketing materials. 
Some Enterprise customers have already given us permission. But in any instance 
where we do not already have explicit consent, reach out to Legal for advice on what 
you need to do to get permission in any specific case. 
Population-focused marketing. While uplifting and focusing on particular populations in 
marketing can be great, there are certain do’s and don’ts to keep in mind.  Don’t ask 
users for and don’t track legally protected class information (e.g., race, religion, 
sexual-orientation, etc.).  What you can do is ask targeted groups (e.g., top-rated 
talent, rising talent, etc.) if they would like to participate in population-focused 
campaigns, and provide a checklist of potential campaigns for them to opt-in to.  You 
will also want to ask them to provide the reason(s) for their interest so you can 
appropriately determine eligibility for your campaign.   
Coalitions, Associations, Group Acronyms. We must avoid using the names of any 
formal associated groups or acronyms that could be confused for these entities.  Even 
if we make up a name (e.g., the “Future of Work Coalition”) we need to check and 
ensure no such group actually exists that corresponds with that name.  We also want 
to make sure no group actually exists with a different name, but that uses the same 
acronym as the made up group name (e.g.  if there was a group called the “Free

Workers’ Committee,” that wouldn’t conflict with “Future of Work Coalition” but the 
acronym for the real group and the made up group would: “FWC”).

might be important to give tips or pointers. If we need to do this, we need to include a

Look, we get it. You all love Upwork. We do too—but we can’t let that love lead to 
overpromising or overshadow the fine print. Accuracy is the word—don’t oversell and 
don’t make promises or guarantees.

requirements and exclusions—it is not a payment guarantee. We know, “we guarantee 
payment” sounds amazing—but it isn’t accurate. In fact, “Hourly Payment Protection”

over. That said, we can accurately talk about how successful most outcomes are on 
Upwork: “X% of clients would recommend Upwork to a friend.” (when based on actual 
evidence; though you may need to get approval from Investor Relations and Legal if 
the stat hasn’t been disclosed before).

profile views? Let’s make sure we have some data backing that up and we are being 
clear about what is being compared.

competitors.  Such statements should be particularly fact-based if used as the risk of 
repercussions from inaccurate statements is much higher than it would be when just 
comparing new and old features of the Upwork platform. 
6.​
Trademark Principles 
A trademark is a word or string of words registered or otherwise established by use to 
represent a particular company or product. One way to establish trademark protection 
is to register the mark, another way is by first developing “secondary meaning” in a 
phrase, which essentially means that a company develops a new, distinct meaning to a 
word or phrase that may already have meaning in common language by using it in 
commercial use to the point that consumers associate the phrase with that company. 
Famous examples include “Apple” as a company name and “Just Do It” (Nike) or “I’m 
Lovin’ It” (McDonald’s) as company mottos. A trademark holder can enforce their mark 
against other companies who may try to market their services through use of the mark 
(i.e. if Wendy’s tried to use “I’m Lovin’ It”). 
Upwork has established trademarks over “Upwork,” “Up We Go,” “Headroom,” “Work 
Without Limits,” “Work Differently,” “Talent Cloud,” “Private Talent Cloud,” “Elance,” 
“Elancer,” and “oDesk”. We are also claiming trademark rights over other marks, 
including “This Is How We Work Now,” and “Upwork It.”  In order to preserve these 
trademarks, we need to adhere to the following principles for use and flexible use of 
Upwork’s marks. …

●​ Use the ® symbol with the first use in an asset of a registered trademark, such 
as Upwork.  
●​ Use the ™ symbol for those where we are seeking trademark status but have 
not yet obtained it through registration, such as TIHWWN, Project Catalog, and 
Virtual Talent Bench.   
●​ Use consistent font or sentence structure (such as title case) across usage for 
the same mark where possible in assets.  
17 
 
●​ If using the mark as a sentence (i.e. “This is how we work now.”), always put the 
™ at the end, even if it’s not the first usage in the asset.

TIHWWN brand mark: 
​If your asset uses “This is how…now”, with different wording than “we work” in 
the middle, we need to include a reference to the full TIHWWN phrasing in close 
proximity in the same asset. You can either: 
​Write out “This is how we work now™” and then mock it up by striking 
through the words you’re replacing and adding them in subscript on top. 
So for Example 3 above, we would write, “This is how we work now™”, 
then cross out “work” and add in subscript above it “hire full time”.  
​Use your variation first and later in the asset (often right afterwards) add, 
This is how we work now™.” So, to comply with this guideline, Example 1 
would become: “This is how we CEO now. This is how we work now™.” 
​If your asset only uses 3 or less words from TIHWWN, such as “This is how” or 
“how __ works,” with no other reference to or words from TIHWWN or 
replacement of other TIHWWN words, it is approved to move forward without a 
requirement for a specific reference to TIHWWN in the same asset (but it doesn’t 
hurt to add it!). Here is an example that mostly is fine based on this guideline, 
but due to the last usage, “how the Fortune 500 works now,” we would need to 
end with “This is how we work now™”: 
 
 
​If your asset is purely for internal purposes and will not be used externally for 
any purpose at any time, we have more flexibility and do not have to follow 
these guidelines as strictly as any use or asset for external purposes.

while driving it forward. 
18 
 
7.​AI Concerns 
Generative AI tools have already begun to revolutionize the tech and business world, 
but with these tools come a number of legal concerns:   
Content Creation 
If Upwork is responsible for the content, Upwork could be liable.  For that reason, we 
must always be sure that, when describing Gen AI tools, we describe them as just 
that–tools—that supplement and support the User’s own work, but do not replace it. 
So, in the example of a Gen AI tool that helps draft a proposal for a User, it is important 
that we don’t describe the tool as drafting the proposal for the user: “Provide some 
basic information and this tool will do the rest, leaving you with a ready-to-send 
proposal.” Instead, the Gen AI tool should always be a support and should be 
described as such: “Get a start on your proposal with some tips from this tool.” 
Intellectual Property Issues 
IP ownership has been one of the major concerns associated with AI tools. The 
concerns are two-fold:  
1.​
Whether the AI tools have or need rights to the content on which they are trained 
2.​
Whether and under what circumstances end-users can claim IP rights over 
content generated by genAI tools 
Our Terms of Service state that users are responsible for ensuring they own any IP 
rights to content they post or otherwise share through Upwork, including work-product. 
This is another reason users must retain control over all their content on Upwork. All 
Product features must ensure that Users: 
●​

●​
Maintain control over both inputs and outputs used in GenAI tools 
Bias Concerns 
If an AI tool has been trained on biased/discriminatory content, the entity responsible 
for the content could be liable for any discriminatory violations.  This again underlines 
the importance of maintaining user control over the ultimate content.  It also means

are not incorporating any biases, including implicit ones. 
Classification Concerns 
While AI tools can be useful in helping users perform their work, we must be careful to 
ensure that providing third-party AI tools to Users does not make freelancers who use 
the Upwork platform appear to be employees. To that end, Upwork’s own AI tools 
cannot be mandatory or direct user’s work too much. Independent contractors like the 
talent on our platform make their own business decisions, including the tools they will 
use to do their work.

UPWORK AD TYPE STYLE GUIDE — Text_On_Visual Copy Rules by Ad Type
==================================================================
BINDING reference for the Upwork Meta Ad Copywriter project (Adrie Etherington,
last updated July 2026). Before writing any on-creative (Text_On_Visual) copy,
identify the ad type from Ad_Format + Visual_Style, locate the matching entry
below, and apply its rules EXACTLY. These rules override all general
Text_On_Visual defaults.

HOW TO USE THIS GUIDE
- Match the brief's Visual_Style to an entry below.
- Apply every rule in that entry — character limits, sentence count, punctuation,
  layout density, and CTA guidance.
- Note the matched entry in the brief summary line
  (e.g., "Ad type resolved to: Chat Bubble — applying Style Guide entry #11").
- If no match is found, apply the closest entry and flag the mismatch. Do not
  silently default to a generic single-headline spec.

GENERAL RULES (apply to ALL entries)
- Follow the Upwork brand voice: clear, concise, supportive, professional.
- 95/5 rule: 95% informative/helpful, 5% subtle personality.
- Use only approved claims and verified statistics.
- Sentence case. No trailing periods on headlines or Text_On_Visual by default.
- Character limits below are editorial intent; where a Figma template slot has a
  tighter HARD cap (see the TEMPLATE CHARACTER LIMITS block in the assignment),
  that cap wins — always fit the slot.


Entry 1 — Split Screen
Layout: A headline at the top above two side-by-side images. The headline is the
only copy element — no body copy, no text on the images. The visual does the work.
Density: Low — one line only.
Rules:
- Write one short, punchy headline. This is the only copy field for this ad type.
- No subhead. No body copy. No text on images.
- Sentence case. No trailing period.
- Two versions: one with a CTA, remaining versions without.
Character limits: Headline with CTA: max 49 · Headline without CTA: max 65 · CTA: max 14
Punctuation: Minimal. Em dashes allowed. No exclamation points. Question marks only if the concept calls for one.
Tone: The headline frames the two images — write as if completing the image's thought.
CTA: Optional. One variant includes a CTA; the rest do not.


Entry 2 — Us vs Them
Layout: Split vertically in an illustrated style. Left = "us" (Upwork/freelancers),
right = "them" (the alternative). Each side: a short headline, 2–3 bullet proof
points, and a short wrap-up line. Extends to ways of working, payment, hiring, etc.
Density: Medium-High.
Rules:
- Headline for each side (left and right).
- 2–3 bullets per side — short, factual, parallel in structure across both sides.
- A one-liner wrap-up beneath the bullets on each side.
- Sentence case. No trailing periods on headlines. Bullets may end without punctuation.
- No CTA on visual unless the brief explicitly requests one.
Character limits: Left headline: max 18 · Right headline: max 18 · Total bullet text per side: max 176 · Left wrap-up: max 31 · Right wrap-up: max 31
Punctuation: Bullets fragment-style, no periods. Wrap-up lines may use an em dash. No exclamation points.
Tone: "Us" = confident, outcome-focused. "Them" = factual, neutral — never mocking. Let the contrast speak.


Entry 3 — Photo with Text (Upwork shell)
Layout: A branded photo of a professional in an Upwork border. A short headline in
the lower left. The photo does the emotional work; the headline anchors the message.
Density: Low — headline only, or headline + short subhead when no CTA.
Rules:
- Write a headline. Short, outcome-led, sentence case, no trailing period.
- Two versions: one with a CTA, remaining versions without.
- When no CTA is used, a subhead may expand the message.
Character limits: Headline (all versions): max 24 · CTA: max 19 · Subhead (no-CTA only): max 43
Punctuation: Minimal. Land cleanly without punctuation where possible.
Tone: Warm and direct. The photo carries the human element — keep the headline crisp and confident.
CTA: Optional. One variant includes a CTA; the rest do not.


Entry 4 — Lifestyle Photo (Full Bleed)
Layout: Full-bleed branded photography — the photo fills the frame, copy sits over it.
Room for a longer headline than most photo formats, but keep density in check.
Density: Low-Medium.
Rules:
- One copy block — a headline or short headline-plus-thought.
- Two versions: one with a CTA, remaining versions without.
- When no CTA is used, the character limit expands.
- Sentence case. No trailing period.
Character limits: Copy with CTA: max 80 · Copy without CTA: max 100 · CTA: max 19
Punctuation: A period is allowed if the copy splits into two distinct sentences. Otherwise avoid trailing punctuation.
Tone: Aspirational but grounded. Match the photo's emotional register.
CTA: Optional. One variant includes a CTA; the rest do not.


Entry 5 — Testimonial
Layout: A real client testimonial with brand elements (stars/badges). Always
includes attribution (name, job title, company).
Density: Medium — quote plus attribution line.
Rules:
- Use a real quote from attached docs or the brief. NEVER fabricate a quote.
- Quotes may be shortened but must not change the intended meaning.
- Always include: first name, last-name initial, job title, and company.
- If no real quote can be sourced and none was provided, use Lorem Ipsum and flag it.
- Sentence case for attribution. No trailing period on attribution.
Character limits: Testimonial copy: max 100 · Credit line (name, title, company): max 51
Punctuation: Opening + closing quotation marks required on the testimonial. Attribution: comma between name/title and title/company.
Tone: Let the quote speak. Do not editorialize or frame it with extra copy.
CTA: Not applicable to visual copy.


Entry 6 — Social Media Profile
Layout: A mockup of a freelancer's social profile — headshot, name (first + last
initial), job title. Left/right columns hold supporting content; a subhead below
the columns is a punchy wrap-up.
Density: Medium-High.
Rules:
- Write left and right column content (skills, outcomes, efficiency, quality, clever lines).
- Write a subhead below the columns — a punchy closer.
- Do NOT write the name or job title (design placeholders / provided).
- Sentence case. No trailing periods.
Character limits: Column left + right combined: max 65 · Subhead: max 28
Punctuation: Fragments OK in columns. Subhead may use an em dash. No exclamation points.
Tone: Clever and professional. Feel authentic, not ad-like — what a skilled freelancer would actually list.
CTA: Not applicable to visual copy.


Entry 7 — Pie Chart
Layout: A circular chart in 4 quadrants — features, benefits, outcomes, or stats.
A center callout ties the quadrants together or adds a branded anchor.
Density: Medium — four quadrant labels + one center callout.
Rules:
- Write four quadrant copy blocks — each a short, distinct point (feature/benefit/stat/outcome).
- Write one center callout (theme-aligned or a branded line, e.g. "Hire smarter").
- All four quadrants parallel in structure (all fragments, or all short phrases — don't mix).
- Sentence case. No trailing periods.
Character limits: Each quadrant: max 30 · Center callout: max 28
Punctuation: Fragments preferred. No periods. Em dashes allowed if warranted.
Tone: Informative and confident. Stats only from approved claims — do not fabricate data.
CTA: Not applicable to visual copy.


Entry 8 — Hybrid
Layout: Lifestyle photography + branded Upwork UI elements tied to the concept.
Always includes a CTA.
Density: Medium — headline, subhead, and CTA. All required.
Rules:
- Write a headline and a subhead. Headline leads; subhead extends/supports.
- Always include a CTA. There are NO no-CTA versions.
- Sentence case. No trailing period on headline or subhead.
Character limits: Headline: max 36 · Subhead: max 60 · CTA: max 22
Punctuation: A period between headline and subhead only if both are complete, distinct sentences. Otherwise avoid.
Tone: The UI grounds the ad — copy should feel like the product in action: confident, specific, outcome-led.
CTA: Required on every variant.


Entry 9 — Search Results
Layout: Three search bars with freelancer role tags inside, each with a hire button.
A headline sits above.
Density: Low-Medium — headline + three talent tags.
Rules:
- One headline. Short, outcome-led or cleverly framed. Sentence case, no trailing period.
- Three talent tags — one per bar. Realistic search terms, written as a user would type them, not marketing language. Pull from Freelancer Work Categories unless the brief specifies.
Character limits: Headline: max 38 · Each talent tag: max 32
Punctuation: No punctuation on talent tags. Headline may use an em dash if warranted.
Tone: The visual demonstrates — the headline frames the payoff cleanly. Tags feel authentic and specific.
CTA: Not specified for visual copy — follow brief or default.


Entry 10 — Text Only
Layout: Text-driven design, maybe a branded background/container. No photo or
illustration — copy carries the full weight.
Density: Medium — three fields, all tightly capped.
Rules:
- Write a headline, subhead, and CTA. All three used.
- Headline lands the core message; subhead extends/proves it; CTA closes.
- Sentence case. No trailing periods on headline or subhead.
- Copy must be especially sharp and self-contained (no visual support).
Character limits: Headline: max 20 · Subhead: max 60 · CTA: max 22
Punctuation: Fragments OK in headline. Subhead may be a complete sentence. Em dash allowed for rhythm.
Tone: Confident and direct. Every word is load-bearing — cut anything that doesn't earn its place.
CTA: Required on every variant.


Entry 11 — Chat Bubble
Layout: TWO chat bubbles simulating a text conversation between two people. One
bubble opens, the second closes. The exchange should sound like a natural
conversation — NOT ad copy, NOT a headline + subtext.
Density: Low — two short copy blocks written as DIALOGUE, not headlines.
Rules:
- Write two chat bubbles: an opening message and a reply.
- Write as a real conversation — casual, natural, direct. Not a headline. Not a tagline.
- The exchange should prove a point, answer a question, or surface a compelling stat about using freelancers or Upwork.
- Sentence case. Conversational punctuation is fine (periods mid-sentence, ellipses if natural). Avoid exclamation points unless genuinely warranted.
Character limits: Chat bubble 1 (opener): max 18 · Chat bubble 2 (reply): max 91
Punctuation: Write as texting — short, natural, human. Full stops OK. Fragments OK.
Tone: Real. Grounded. Two people who sound like actual humans, not brand voices. The format creates trust — the copy just has to not break it.
CTA: Not applicable to visual copy.


Entry 12 — Notification
Layout: An ad that looks like an app notification. Copy mimics a real notification.
Always includes a CTA.
Density: Low — headline + CTA only.
Rules:
- Write copy that reads like an ACTUAL app notification — hint at hiring a freelancer, finding talent, or a successful Upwork outcome, WITHOUT reading like an ad.
- Always include a CTA. There are NO no-CTA versions.
- Sentence case. No trailing period on the notification copy.
Character limits: Headline (notification copy): max 52 · CTA: max 12
Punctuation: Notification-style — clean and direct. A period is OK if it reads as a complete sentence. Avoid exclamation points.
Tone: Functional and believable — like something that actually popped up on a phone. If it reads like an ad, rewrite it.
CTA: Required on every variant.


Entry 13 — Reminder
Layout: A mobile app pop-up reminder. Short, direct, action-oriented. Always a CTA.
Density: Low — one copy block + CTA.
Rules:
- Write copy that reads like a real reminder notification, tied to working with freelancers, hiring on Upwork, or a specific outcome.
- Keep it short — the format demands brevity.
- Always include a CTA. There are NO no-CTA versions.
- Sentence case. Punctuation OK if it aids clarity.
Character limits: Copy: max 52 · CTA: max 20
Punctuation: A period is fine for a complete-sentence reminder. Keep it clean.
Tone: Practical and believable — like something a user set for themselves. Upwork connection feels natural, not forced.
CTA: Required on every variant.


Entry 14 — Device UI (Photo)
Layout: A device (phone/laptop) showing Upwork's platform/UI. A headline appears
at the top above the device.
Density: Low — headline only.
Rules:
- One headline, relating to the UI shown on the device.
- Sentence case. No trailing period.
- The headline frames what the viewer sees — it should make them want to look closer.
Character limits: Headline: max 38
Punctuation: Minimal. Em dash allowed if warranted.
Tone: Confident and specific. The device + UI demonstrate — the headline anchors the payoff.
CTA: Not specified for visual copy — follow brief or default.


Entry 15 — Platform UI
Layout: A featured moment from the Upwork platform (homepage, search page, Uma
interface). The headline relates to the specific UI feature. CTA optional.
Density: Low — headline + optional subhead, expanding when no CTA.
Rules:
- Write a headline and subhead, both relating to the UI feature shown.
- Two versions: one with a CTA, remaining versions without.
- When no CTA, combined room increases by 16 characters (distribute as needed).
- Sentence case. No trailing periods.
Character limits (with CTA): Headline: max 25 · Subhead: max 18 · CTA: max 16
Character limits (without CTA): +16 characters distributed between headline and subhead as needed.
Punctuation: Minimal — copy should feel like a clean label for what's shown.
Tone: Platform-native — copy belongs in the product, not on top of it.
CTA: Optional. One variant includes a CTA; the rest do not.


Entry 16 — Meme
Layout: A viral meme format carrying key messaging. Copy usually prompted or
requested in the brief.
Density: Low — headline only, but tone carries the weight.
Rules:
- Write copy that fits the meme format referenced in the brief.
- If no specific meme format is provided, flag it — meme copy structure depends on the format.
- Copy should feel native to the meme — if it reads like an ad, it fails.
- Sentence case where natural; meme formats sometimes use intentional capitalization as part of the joke — follow the format convention.
Character limits: Headline: max 43
Punctuation: Follow the meme format's conventions — format-dependent.
Tone: Witty and culturally aware. Don't force Upwork messaging into a meme awkwardly — find the angle that earns the format.
CTA: Not typically used on the visual — follow brief if specified.


Entry 17 — Sticky Note
Layout: A sticky note with a title at top and listed items below — single column
or two columns. Checklist, comparison, us-vs-them, or feature/benefit.
Density: Medium — title + column content. Layout varies by version.
Rules:
- Write a title (headline) and column content.
- Write at least one single-column and one double-column version per concept.
- Column content is list-style — short items, parallel structure. Checkmarks, dashes, or plain text depending on the concept.
- Sentence case. No trailing periods on list items.
Character limits (double-column): Headline: max 12 · Column A + B combined: max 136
Character limits (single-column): Headline: max 26 · Single column content: max 112
Punctuation: List items are fragments — no periods. Title may use minimal punctuation if warranted.
Tone: Practical and visual — like something someone actually wrote down, not a polished brand statement.
CTA: Not applicable to visual copy.


Entry 18 — Poll
Layout: A background image with a poll bar overlaid — stats, mock results, or
comparisons. Always includes a CTA.
Density: Medium — headline, subhead/stat, and CTA.
Rules:
- Write a headline and a subhead or stat line. The poll bar carries the data; the headline frames it.
- Content may be prompted by the brief or generated from approved Upwork stats.
- Always include a CTA. There are NO no-CTA versions.
- Sentence case. No trailing period on headline.
Character limits: Headline: max 36 · Subhead/stat: max 75 · CTA: max 12
Punctuation: Stats may use a colon or em dash to separate number from label. Headline stays clean.
Tone: Data-led where possible. Stats from approved claims only. A mock poll must feel believable and relevant to the SMB audience.
CTA: Required on every variant.


Entry 19 — Tweet / Post Mockup
Layout: A mockup of a tweet or social post — organic social content, a veiled ad
that reads like a real post.
Density: Medium — one copy block, moderate length.
Rules:
- Write copy that reads like a REAL social post, not an ad.
- The Upwork connection should feel natural and earned — not brand-inserted.
- Sentence case. Conversational punctuation is fine.
- Do NOT include handles, hashtags, or platform UI elements in the copy — those are design elements.
Character limits: Copy: max 115
Punctuation: Write as a real post — periods, natural line breaks, light punctuation. No exclamation points unless the voice calls for one.
Tone: Authentic and human. Lives or dies on whether it reads like something a real person would post. If it sounds like an ad, rewrite it.
CTA: Not applicable to visual copy.


Entry 20 — Text with Button and Cursor
Layout: A UI-style ad with a button element and a cursor clicking it. The copy is
INSIDE the button — the button copy is the entire message.
Density: Minimal — one copy element only.
Rules:
- Write copy for the button/CTA only. This is the sole copy field.
- Must be verb-led — it is both the message and the call to action.
- Feel like a real UI button — action-oriented and specific.
- Sentence case. No trailing period.
Character limits: CTA / button copy: max 15
Punctuation: None. Buttons don't have punctuation.
Tone: Direct and action-forward. In 15 characters, imply a benefit and prompt a click.
CTA: The button copy IS the CTA. No separate CTA field.


Entry 21 — Talent Profile
Layout: A freelancer profile card with a headline at the top. The profile is the
visual element; the headline is the primary copy.
Density: Low — headline only, plus optional CTA.
Rules:
- One headline, relating to the profile shown and framing the value of finding talent on Upwork.
- Two versions with a CTA; remaining versions (out of 6) without.
- Sentence case. No trailing period.
Character limits: Headline: max 36 · CTA: max 21
Punctuation: Minimal. Em dash allowed if warranted.
Tone: Confident and specific. The profile is the visual proof — the headline makes the viewer want to hire.
CTA: Optional. Two variants include a CTA; the rest do not.


Entry 22 — Bespoke
Layout: A custom layout built from scratch — no fixed structure.
Density: Variable — determined by the brief's described layout.
Rules:
- Copy is variable. Read the brief for layout description, visual references, creative direction.
- Identify the closest matching ad type and apply those structural rules as a starting point.
- One variant includes a CTA; the rest without, unless the brief specifies otherwise.
- Sentence case throughout. All other formatting guardrails apply.
Character limits: Text: variable — use judgment based on the layout density described in the brief.
Tone: Fully brief-dependent. Default to the core voice: clear, outcome-led, grounded.
CTA: Optional. One variant includes a CTA; the rest do not — unless the brief specifies.


Entry 23 — Illustration
Layout: Illustrations tied to the ad theme. The illustration carries the visual
concept; copy complements it.
Density: Low — headline + optional CTA.
Rules:
- One headline, connecting to the illustration theme and landing the core message.
- One variant includes a CTA; remaining versions without.
- Sentence case. No trailing period.
Character limits: Headline: max 38 · CTA: max 16
Punctuation: Minimal. Let illustration and headline work together cleanly.
Tone: Match the illustration — playful illustration, playful headline; bold/graphic illustration, tight/confident headline.
CTA: Optional. One variant includes a CTA; the rest do not.


Entry 24 — Carousel
Layout: A multi-slide ad. Each slide has its own headline. The final slide always
includes a CTA. Default 3–4 slides unless the brief specifies.
Density: Low per slide — one headline each; the narrative builds across slides.
Rules:
- Write a headline for each slide — each unique, each connected to the overall theme.
- Default output: two versions with 4 slides, one version with 3 slides (per concept).
- Longer carousels are specified in the brief with extra guidance.
- The FINAL slide must always include a CTA.
- Headlines flow as a progression — don't repeat the same thought across slides.
- Sentence case. No trailing periods.
Character limits: Each slide headline: max 36 · Final slide CTA: max 22
Punctuation: Minimal per slide. Em dashes allowed. Headlines are distinct beats, not fragments of one sentence.
Tone: Narrative and progressive — each slide makes the viewer want the next. The final slide closes and converts.
CTA: Required on the final slide only. All other slides: no CTA.

UPWORK PAID ACQUISITION — PER-VISUAL-STYLE IMAGE GENERATION RULES
===================================================================

These rules define what the AI image generator (Gemini) should produce
for each visual style, and how the image should be composed to sit
correctly inside the Figma template's image-slot layer.

General rules for ALL styles:
- Never generate text, logos, or watermarks in the image
- Leave adequate negative space at edges where brand elements will sit
- Warm, natural lighting preferred over flat or harsh light
- Photorealistic unless style explicitly calls for illustration
- No faces with distorted features — if generating people, quality matters
- Images should feel professional, modern, and on-brand for Upwork
- Default color palette: warm neutrals, Upwork green (#14a800) accents welcome


1. GRAPHIC WITH TEXT
   Image type: Illustrated graphic or abstract visual element
   Composition: Graphic occupies 40-60% of frame, leaving clear space for text
   Subject: Abstract shapes, icons, or stylized illustrations related to work/hiring
   Negative space: Required on left or right side for headline
   DO NOT: Generate photorealistic images. This style uses illustration.

2. SPLIT SCREEN
   Image type: Two distinct photographs or scenes
